paras: The threatened lynching of William Woods took place in Sherman, Texas, in June 1888, when a crowd threatened to lynch Woods, a young Black man jailed on a charge of assaulting Mrs. Maggie Miles, a white servant. Officers brought him into the jail under guard, and reports of a likely alibi led the crowd to hold back. One Austin paper nevertheless headlined that he had been "Strung Up to a Tree," a claim its own text did not support.

Miles, who worked and lived in a servant's room at the residence of J. R. Cole, said that about 3 a.m. on June 7 a man entered through an open window, threatened her with a knife or razor, assaulted her, and fled. She named Woods, who had worked as a porter at Sam Lazarus's house next door, although he had left Sherman for Dallas on the Tuesday before. The Sherman correspondent also linked the case to the murder of Genie Watkins at Gainesville the year before, noting that Miles had once worked for the Watkins family.

On the evening of June 8, City Marshal Blaine and Deputy Sheriff Whitesides arrived from Dallas with Woods. According to the Sherman dispatch, "great excitement prevailed" and "strong fears of lynching were entertained," but the sheriff took the prisoner to jail by a roundabout route under strong guard, and few people knew he had arrived until he was locked up. The same dispatch said the probability of an alibi caused "the enraged populace to desist until further investigations," and added that if he proved guilty "lynching will be inevitable."

By June 9 no identification had taken place, because Miles was ill, though she still insisted that Woods was the man. The correspondent reported that the determination to lynch Woods "if guilty" remained strong but that evidence pointing to his innocence held the crowd back. Judge Nat Gunter of Sherman was to testify that he had seen Woods in Dallas at 9 p.m. on the night of the assault, too late to reach Sherman by train, and the theory was put forward that Miles had mistaken another man for him in the dark.

No report of Miles's identification of Woods, or of his release, was found. On July 7 the San Antonio Daily Light reported that the trial of "the negro Carson, for outraging Mrs. Maggie Miles" was going on at Sherman, with important witnesses on both sides. The brief does not explain the different name, and no report of a verdict appears in the coverage.

All of the June coverage traces to the Sherman correspondent's two dispatches, printed as specials by the Fort Worth Daily Gazette on June 9 and 10 and by the Austin Weekly Statesman on June 14. The Gazette headlined the first "A Black Fiend" and "Threats of Lynching," and the text called the attacker "the black demon" while treating a lynching as certain should Woods prove guilty. The follow-up dispatch also set out the alibi at length and the theory that Miles was mistaken.

The Statesman printed the first dispatch under the headline "A Demon" and "The East Texas Negro Rape Fiend Caught and Strung Up to a Tree," although the text beneath said only that Woods had been jailed and the crowd had desisted. On another page of the same issue it ran the June 9 dispatch under the milder heading "The Sherman Outrage."

Only the Statesman headline says Woods was hanged; the dispatch under it, the Gazette's version of the same text, and the June 9 follow-up all report him alive in jail. The accused's name also differs: the June dispatches name William Woods, while the July trial brief names a man called Carson.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of William Woods
bases: A Sherman crowd was reported ready to lynch a Black man jailed on a charge of assaulting a white woman and held off only by a guarded transfer and a probable alibi, a threatened lynching with no killing (A1, A2).

The 'enraged populace' threatened to lynch Woods over an alleged assault, but no report says he was seized, harmed or killed; he remained in jail and later reports speak of a trial (A1, A2, A5). The Statesman headline 'Strung Up to a Tree' is contradicted by its own text (A4).

The arrest and the lynching threats come from one Sherman correspondent's dispatches of June 8 and 9, printed by the Fort Worth Gazette and the Austin Statesman (A1, A2, A3, A4); a separate July brief confirms only that a trial for the assault on Mrs. Miles was held, under another name (A5).

accounts.label: Sherman correspondent, June 8
accounts.gist: Woods was jailed on Miles's identification; fears of lynching ran high, but the guarded transfer and a probable alibi caused the crowd to desist, and lynching would be 'inevitable' if he proved guilty.

accounts.label: Sherman correspondent, June 9
accounts.gist: Miles had not yet seen Woods but insisted he was the man; witnesses including Judge Nat Gunter placed him in Dallas, and the theory was that Miles had mistaken another man for him.

accounts.label: Austin Statesman headline
accounts.gist: The headline over the June 8 telegram said the 'Negro Rape Fiend' was 'Caught and Strung Up to a Tree'.

accounts.label: State-news brief
accounts.gist: A man called Carson was on trial at Sherman in July for outraging Mrs. Maggie Miles.

framing.detail: The Gazette headlined 'A Black Fiend' and 'Threats of Lynching' and called the attacker a 'black demon', presenting lynching as 'inevitable' if Woods proved guilty, while also reporting alibi evidence that pointed to his innocence.
The Austin Statesman ran both Sherman telegrams, the first under the headline 'The East Texas Negro Rape Fiend Caught and Strung Up to a Tree', which its text did not support.
